Testing the Job Processor

slaScan.job.test.js mocks the whole service away — this file has nothing to test except that it wired the two together correctly.

jobs/slaScan.job.js has almost no logic of its own — it reads env.SLA_BREACH_HOURS, calls escalateOverdueTickets, and reshapes the result. Testing it doesn't need Prisma mocked, fake timers, or anything ticket.service.test.js already covers — it needs the service mocked instead, so the test can check the glue on its own:

// Figure 6.13: mocking the service, not Prisma (tests/unit/slaScan.job.test.js)
const mockEscalateOverdueTickets = jest.fn();

jest.unstable_mockModule('../../src/services/ticket.service.js', () => ({
  escalateOverdueTickets: mockEscalateOverdueTickets,
}));

const { default: processSlaScan } = await import('../../src/jobs/slaScan.job.js');

it('escalates using the configured SLA threshold and reports how many tickets it escalated', async () => {
  mockEscalateOverdueTickets.mockResolvedValue(2);

  const result = await processSlaScan();

  expect(mockEscalateOverdueTickets).toHaveBeenCalledWith(env.SLA_BREACH_HOURS);
  expect(result).toEqual({ escalatedCount: 2 });
});

Same jest.unstable_mockModule + dynamic import() pattern every other test in this suite uses to swap out a real dependency (Week 2/3), just aimed at a different module than usual — services/ticket.service.js instead of config/db.js. This is the same layering argument as "The Escalation Service Function" earlier in this lesson, seen from the test side: because the real logic lives in a service function slaScan.job.js merely calls, testing the job only means testing that it calls that function correctly — the threshold it reads, and the shape it returns — and nothing about tickets, Prisma, or events needs to appear in this file at all.
